summary.en: In late-1960s San Francisco a full psychedelic subcultural scene took shape—venues, radio, shops, and more. They were also early products of rock culture.
summary.zh: 1960年代末的旧金山，出现了一整套关于迷幻的亚文化场景，包括专门的演出场所、电台、商店等等。它们也是摇滚文化的早期产物。

body.zh:
1960年代末的旧金山，出现了一整套关于迷幻的亚文化场景，包括专门的演出场所、电台、商店等等。它们也是摇滚文化的早期产物。

现在我们来看看旧金山，以及其中的Haight Ashbury如何在60年代末成为迷幻运动的核心地带。我之前提到过亚文化 (sub culture) ，它在流行音乐中自有一套机制。许多学者都对亚文化很感兴趣，因为借此可以进入一种足够小众的文化，从而理解音乐如何塑造认同感、价值观等理念。很多学者都研究过亚文化。谈及早期Haight Ashbury相关的迷幻事物，我们所讲的就是亚文化，因为很多情况下我们真的不知道那里发生了什么，除了稍后会讲到的1967年初的“Human be-in”事件。但可以确定的是，到了67年的夏天也即“爱之夏”（the summer of love），Scott McKenzie所唱的“你头戴花朵来到旧金山”之类的东西受到欢迎，这时旧金山真的开始进入主流视野了。旧金山迷幻文化的历史可以追溯到1965年，也即它进入主流视野的2年之前。在这2年时间里，它就是一个亚文化场景。

如前所述，旧金山的迷幻文化源于Haight Ashbury附近。这块地方有一些很棒的19世纪风格的街区，还有一条贯穿其中的商业街叫做Haight，以及一条与之相交的、直通金门公园的街道叫做Ashbury。走到Haight Ashbury的边缘，穿过那条街就到金门公园了。那是当地一个很棒的公园，在旧金山生活的人离不开它。那是个闲逛的好地方。迷幻文化的萌芽，也即LSD的服用、“神游”以及聚众吃LSD听音乐的派对，其实可以发现于1965年夏天内华达州的Virginia City。那么，就在The Beatles经历了第一次“牙医体验”（按George Harrison的说法）之后没几个月，许多学生都来到此地某个被称作Red Dog Saloon的地方。不需要太长的车程就能到那儿。他们一边服药，一边听着The Charlatans等艺人的歌。这就是迷幻派对的真正雏形。

说回旧金山，1965年的夏末秋初出现了第一批迷幻活动。有个自称The Family Dog的群体组织了许多的此类活动。他们会组织一些夜场活动、请几个乐队出场，还有灯光表演等等，我是说一切与旧金山的迷幻活动相关的东西。他们活跃于Longshoreman’s Halls或者任何租价低廉的场所，并将那些夜场活动称作“A Tribute to Dr. Strange”或者另一个我很喜欢的名字“A Tribute to Sparkle Plenty”。你可以看到为这些活动准备的海报，日后常见的旧金山迷幻式海报艺术就此形成。记住，我们讲的是1965年的秋天；如果不在当地，你就无法知道这一切的发生。这并不是全国性或者世界性的现象，它仅仅发生于Haight Ashbury附近。你必须身处当地，才能知晓这些事情。

这其中有一个很重要的人物——作者Ken Kesey。《飞越疯人院》是他的经典小说之一。Tom Wolfe的《The Electric Kool-Aid Acid Test》讲述的，基本上就是Ken Kesey和他的那些人称the Merry Pranksters之类的追随者。他们周游四方，通过巴士在城镇间穿梭。那是一辆带有迷幻风格涂鸦的巴士。大多数巴士的目的地是底特律、芝加哥或者波士顿之类，但他们的大巴只写着“远方”，因为它就是要把人们带到更远的地方。每到一个城镇，他们就发出传单，告诉大家即将在城市边缘举办“迷幻测试”——那里是法外之地。花上1美元，你就可以加入其中，买点迷幻药、彻夜“神游”。他们就像是迷幻界的Johnny Appleseed【注】，活跃于旧金山附近开车可达的地方。

注：Johnny Appleseed，美国拓荒者，在推广苹果种植方面颇有贡献。其“apple seed”之名号也是由此而来。

我曾说过，可以从两个方面来看待LSD。其一是更加理想主义的方面。比如说Timothy Leary，这个受过心理学、精神病学训练的人，写了一本叫做《A Psychedelic Experience》的书。也许他受了Aldous Huxley《The Doors of Perception》的部分影响，不过Leary写的是有关迷幻体验的临床医学书。他对孩子们说，要懂得进入“状态”，也要懂得脱离“状态”；他真正想做的是提高他们的意识。Ken Kesey和Merry Pranksters则只想要享乐。他们有点像达达主义者，反对成规，个性有点疯狂。总之，年轻人开始沉醉于LSD、反主流文化和迷幻体验。这里所说的年轻人并非青少年，而是家住那一带的达到大学年纪或更年长的人。1967年1月，他们举行了名为“human be-in”的活动，算是“humanbeing”和“human be-in”的谐音。“be-in”这一形式逐渐流行起来，人们尝试使用各种“in”，比如“sit-in”、“love-in”以及Rowan和Martin主持的节目《laugh-in》。什么东西都成了一种“in”，不过首创者就是“human be-in”。他们做了所谓的“部落聚集”，也即把音乐和艾伦·金斯堡等垮掉派诗人汇于一处。在场的还有大量制作迷幻药的Owsley Stanley，以及Timothy Leary。这些人在金门公园聚集起来，举行了这场盛大的免费狂欢。这算是反主流文化的开端。它引起了全国媒体的报道，人们不能相信会有这些疯狂的家伙在旧金山干着疯狂的勾当。当然了，他们把一切都归责于那些该死的药，认为其让年轻人失去了理智。不论如何，这是我们第一次看到亚文化受到全国性的关注。

其后，Bill Graham开办了“The Fillmore”，它是承办迷幻活动和音乐会的至关重要的场地。Chet Helms则开办了“Avalon Ballroom”。这样一来就有了两个专门的音乐会场地，配有精心设计的灯光和音响，可供打造迷幻 的夜晚。所以这一切开始变得有组织起来。事实上，Fillmore和Avalon成了后来遍布全国的乐队演出场所的原型。在那个时候，the Beatles等乐队只能在体育场做演出；乐队做演出的地方，从来就不是为摇滚音乐会设计的。但是有了Fillmore、有了Avalon，你可以在专门为摇滚音乐会设计的场地表演了。

同样在当时的旧金山，曾参与AM电台开发的Tom Donahue想到，要是有一个完全按DJ的心意来播放音乐的电台就好了。这是top 40电台中无法实现的事情。那么，他希望能找到一个可用的、便宜的电台。那时FM电台尚未广泛投入使用，大多是被宗教组织用于布道，或是被大学用于函授课程，又或是播放古典音乐。很多人的收音机上甚至没有FM频道，汽车上也是如此。然后，Tom Donahue致电本地的各个FM电台，直到他发现有一家电台的电话打不通。他想：如果连电话费都付不起，那么他们的经营状况肯定很糟糕；我要和他们谈谈，我打赌他们不会反对我来做节目。于是他开始广播，从自己的专辑收藏里选择了那些无法拿到AM电台上播放的东西。结果Haight Ashbury的人们都来收听这个频道。总之，FM电台发展的基础就是这种自由的形式和专辑导向（album oriented）的理念。我是说，DJ可以自由决定做一期以飞翔为主题的节目，然后翻查自己的收藏，找出他认为与飞翔有关的歌曲来播放。当然也可以是别的主题，或者根本就没有主题。优秀的吉他solo也行，只要你愿意。这有点迷幻，对吧？然后Haight Ashbury的人就开始收听了，FM电台这种形式在他们之间流行起来。就像所有流行的东西一样，在你还未察觉时，就有人参与进来然后发现其中的生财之道。进入70年代，全国都有FM电台了，而真正的起点就是旧金山。同期也有其他FM自由式电台诞生，因此不能说这仅仅发生在旧金山，但是Tom Donahue促成的一切确实重要。

市面上还首次出现了专注于摇滚文化的杂志。一直以来都有《Teen Beat》之类的青少年杂志，封面上是Paul McCartney、Peter Noon等人的照片。而现在所说的是最早的《The Oracle》或后来的《Rolling Stone》等等，它们都出自旧金山，真正专注于音乐本身及其周边文化。首家迷幻用品商店也出现在旧金山，最重要的是，在其中你能够得到音乐、珠帘、焚香、香炉、全套的服药装备、卷纸、水烟枪等等，你所要的东西应有尽有。它照顾到了嬉皮文化的需要。不久之后，到60年代末、70年代初，全国各地都能找到迷幻用品店了。这些商店成了各地的反主流文化的大本营，但它的一大起源就是旧金山。

以上是旧金山亚文化的大致面貌。在下一节，我们将谈谈这种旧金山文化下的重要乐队。
body.en:
In late-1960s San Francisco a full psychedelic subcultural scene took shape—venues, radio, shops, and more. They were also early products of rock culture.

Now San Francisco, and how Haight-Ashbury became the core of the psychedelic movement in the late 1960s. I mentioned subculture earlier; it has its own mechanisms in popular music. Many scholars study subcultures because they open a small enough culture to see how music shapes identity, values, and related ideas. Early Haight-Ashbury psychedelia is subculture: often we simply did not know what was happening there, except for the early-1967 Human Be-In we will cover. What is clear: by summer 1967—the Summer of Love—when Scott McKenzie’s “If You’re Going to San Francisco” (flowers in your hair) caught on, San Francisco truly entered the mainstream view. The history of San Francisco psychedelia goes back to 1965, two years before that mainstream moment. For those two years it was a subcultural scene.

As said, it grew around Haight-Ashbury: fine nineteenth-century neighborhoods, a commercial street named Haight, and Ashbury crossing it toward Golden Gate Park. At the edge of Haight-Ashbury, across the street, is Golden Gate Park—a great local park San Franciscans live with, a good place to hang out. The sprouts of psychedelic culture—LSD use, “trips,” and parties of taking LSD and listening to music—can be found in summer 1965 in Virginia City, Nevada. Only months after the Beatles’ first “dentist experience” (George Harrison’s phrase), many students went to a place called the Red Dog Saloon. Not a long drive. They took drugs and listened to acts like the Charlatans. That was the real prototype of the psychedelic party.

Back in San Francisco, the first psychedelic events appeared in late summer and early autumn 1965. A group calling itself the Family Dog organized many such nights—bands, light shows, everything tied to San Francisco psychedelic events. They worked Longshoreman’s Hall and any cheap rentals, under names like “A Tribute to Dr. Strange” or one I like, “A Tribute to Sparkle Plenty.” You can see the posters; the familiar San Francisco psychedelic poster art formed then. Remember: autumn 1965. If you were not local, you would not know. This was not a national or world phenomenon—only around Haight-Ashbury. You had to be there.

An important figure: writer Ken Kesey. One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest is among his classic novels. Tom Wolfe’s The Electric Kool-Aid Acid Test is basically about Kesey and followers called the Merry Pranksters. They traveled by bus between towns—a bus with psychedelic graffiti. Most buses go to Detroit, Chicago, or Boston; theirs just said “Further,” because it was meant to take people farther. In each town they handed out flyers for an “Acid Test” at the edge of town—outside the law. For a dollar you could join, buy some acid, trip all night. They were like the Johnny Appleseed of psychedelia, active within driving range of San Francisco.

Note: Johnny Appleseed was an American frontiersman who helped spread apple growing; the name comes from that.

I said LSD can be seen two ways. One is more idealistic—Timothy Leary, trained in psychology and psychiatry, wrote The Psychedelic Experience. He may have drawn partly on Aldous Huxley’s The Doors of Perception, but Leary wrote a clinical book on the psychedelic experience. He told young people to learn to turn on and turn off; he really wanted to raise consciousness. Ken Kesey and the Merry Pranksters mainly wanted fun. A bit like Dadaists—anti-convention, a little wild. Anyway, young people began to immerse in LSD, counterculture, and psychedelic experience. Not teens, but college-age or older people living in that area. In January 1967 they held a “Human Be-In”—a play on “human being” and “be-in.” The “be-in” form caught on: sit-in, love-in, Rowan and Martin’s Laugh-In. Everything became an “in,” but the Human Be-In came first. They held a “tribal gathering” of music and Beat poets like Allen Ginsberg. Owsley Stanley, who made a lot of acid, was there, and Timothy Leary. They gathered in Golden Gate Park for a huge free celebration. That counts as a start of the counterculture. National media covered it; people could not believe these crazy folks in San Francisco doing crazy things. Of course they blamed the damn drugs for making youth lose their minds. Either way, it was the first time the subculture got national attention.

Then Bill Graham opened the Fillmore, a crucial venue for psychedelic events and concerts. Chet Helms opened the Avalon Ballroom. Two dedicated concert halls, with carefully designed lights and sound for psychedelic nights. Things got organized. In fact Fillmore and Avalon became prototypes for rock venues nationwide. At that time bands like the Beatles only played stadiums; performance spaces had never been designed for rock concerts. With Fillmore and Avalon you could play rooms built for rock.

Also in San Francisco then, Tom Donahue—who had worked in AM radio—thought: what if a station played music entirely by the DJ’s taste? Impossible on Top 40. He wanted a usable, cheap station. FM was not widely used yet—mostly churches for sermons, universities for distance courses, or classical. Many radios, including car radios, had no FM. Donahue called local FM stations until one did not answer. He figured: if they cannot pay the phone bill, they must be in bad shape; talk to them—they will not mind me doing a show. He went on air, picking from his own collection what AM would not play. Haight-Ashbury people tuned in. The basis of FM growth was that freeform, album-oriented idea. A DJ could do a show on flying, dig through the collection for songs about flying—or any theme, or none. A great guitar solo, if you wanted. A bit psychedelic, right? Haight-Ashbury listened; FM caught on among them. As with anything popular, before you notice, someone sees how to make money. By the 1970s FM was nationwide; the real start was San Francisco. Other freeform FM stations arose elsewhere too, so it was not only San Francisco—but what Donahue set in motion mattered.

Magazines focused on rock culture also appeared first. There had long been teen magazines like Teen Beat with Paul McCartney or Peter Noone on the cover. Now came the earliest Oracle and later Rolling Stone and so on—out of San Francisco, really about the music and its surrounding culture. The first head shops also appeared there: music, bead curtains, incense, burners, full drug kits, rolling papers, water pipes—whatever you needed for hippie culture. Soon, by the late 1960s and early 1970s, head shops were everywhere; they became local counterculture bases, but a major origin was San Francisco.

That is the rough face of the San Francisco subculture. Next section: important bands in that culture.
